newsitem.title: UK: Study findings could help save endangered turtles.
newsitem.headline: Study findings could help save endangered turtles.

text.p: German researchers said on Wednesday new findings about the migration patterns of the endangered loggerhead turtles could provide a key to helping environmentalists save rare turtle species.

In a recent study, Werner Schroth and his colleagues at Goethe University in Frankfurt found that loggerhead turtles go home every year to breed not only to the same region, where they were born, but to the very same beaches.
Writing in the science journal, Nature, they said they had collected tissue samples from 81 dead baby turtles on beaches across Greece and Turkey.

The loggerheads have been migrating there to lay their eggs for hundreds of thousands of years. They are known to swim thousands of kilometres (miles) to their nesting sites and seek the same region year after year.
Schroth's group found clear genetic evidence that the turtles were returning not just to the same general area, but to the same beach where they were born.

"The consequences for conservation management are obvious. The pre-programmed female reproductive behaviour makes it unlikely that the loss of a breeding habitat (because of human building operations, for example) can be compensated for by emigration to other colonies," they wrote.
"Thus, to preserve the genetic diversity of the (turtle population) one needs to preserve individual nesting sites," Schroth and his colleagues wrote.
It was not clear, they said, whether transferring eggs from one nest to another in an attempt to get turtles to accept a new nesting site would work.
Last month, researchers reported leatherback turtles follow almost identical routes when emigrating. Turtles are believed to use magnetic as well as environmental clues to navigate.
